ANSPDCP completed an investigation in August 2026 at Global Customer Care Services S.R.L., started after the company notified a personal data breach. A cyber attack on its infrastructure affected the confidentiality and availability of personal data of many employees, former employees and others. The authority found the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures, including regular testing of their effectiveness. It fined the company RON 26,294 (EUR 5,000) and ordered it to implement access monitoring and logging systems with log retention of at least 30 days.

Following a complaint from an individual, the Romanian authority investigated a company that used a time-and-attendance and access control system based on employees' fingerprints. It found that biometric data of employees was processed without a legal basis under Article 9 and in breach of data minimisation, since less intrusive alternatives could achieve the same purposes. The company was fined 26,236 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered to replace the biometric system with a non-biometric solution.
The DPA issued a warning concerning the implementation by a controller of an AI tool intended to be used employment and promotion purposes.

The DPA fined an IT company providing digital HR and occupational health services SEK 1,800,000 (€160,000) for a failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures following a data breach affecting over 2 million individuals.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision in an own-volition inquiry into Google's processing of location data in Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020. It found infringements concerning lawfulness and fairness, accountability, transparency and retention of location data. It imposed administrative fines totalling €403 million and ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance within 6 months. The full decision was to be issued later; this text is only the press release.

The DPA fined a Member of Parliament €6,000 for failing to cooperate with the DPA under Article 31 GDPR, particularly after he refused to fully comply with repeated requests to temporarily suspend the operations of his online platform "Agora".

The social services department requested a service provider to provide numerous information concerning disabled people for which it received funds. The DPA held that requesting this information would be disproportionate and not sufficiently transparent.

The DPA issued a reprimand against a journalist for failing to comply with the data minimisation principle, by publishing a court decision on his social media account without properly redacting the name of the accused.

The DPA investigated the Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure for sending a message to the general public via SMS without prior information or consent. The DPA held that the transmission was lawful as it was carried out in the public interest; i.e. to raise awareness for road safety.

The DPA fined CaixaBank €408,000 for a violation of the data protection by design principle since the bank’s standard process in inheritance cases required heirs to provide more information than necessary.

The Romanian DPA fined a bedding retailer RON 10,517 (€2,000) for infringing Article 21 GDPR by continuing to send marketing calls and SMS messages after the data subject exercised their right to object.
The DPA ordered a city to ensure that the personal data of pupils collected when using digital learning tools are only processed to fulfil the controller’s educational obligations.

A customer complained that the bank's Italian branch kept sending in-app marketing notifications although he had switched them off in the app and told customer service. The cause was a missing synchronisation between internal systems and the CRM unit; at least ten unwanted notifications were sent between October 2025 and May 2026. The Garante found breaches of the fairness/transparency principle and Articles 12, 21 and 24, partly because customer service wrongly told the complainant that notifications could not be removed. It ordered corrective measures and a fine of EUR 5,508,000, and ordered publication.

A hospital employee complained about access to her health dossier at the Friuli Centrale University Health Authority. A colleague checked her Covid-19 test status through the dossier on the medical management's instruction to organise ward shifts, and other staff with no care relationship also opened it. The Garante found the dossier was configured unlawfully: it allowed non-care uses, had no automatic access alerts, and used one 30-minute inactivity lock for all devices. It ordered corrective measures within 60 days and a fine of EUR 24,000, and ordered publication.

The Garante learned from press reports and complaints that video surveillance cameras were installed in the changing rooms of a swimming pool run by the Trento sports facilities company. The cameras, active since 2007, filmed the lockers to prevent theft and kept images for 72 hours. The Garante found no valid legal basis and disproportionate processing, insufficient transparency towards users and workers (signs only at the entrance, workers informed only in June 2026) and excessive retention. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000 and ordered publication; no further corrective measures were needed because the cameras had been switched off and removed.

Two employees of the national metrology institute complained about a video surveillance system at its Turin site that had been switched on in test mode without proper transparency and not as agreed with the unions. The Garante found that the institute ran the system on four working days with more cameras (18 instead of 10) and different placement than agreed with the unions, without employee information notices, with a deficient first-level sign, no second-level notice and no DPIA. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 12, 13, 35 and 88 GDPR plus Italian Code Articles 2-ter and 114. It fined the institute EUR 10,000 and ordered publication, imposing no further corrective measures because the conduct had ended. The complaint point about monitor placement was not upheld.

A municipality under extraordinary administration passed on the name of a person who had sent a generic email asking to meet the commissioners about alleged mismanagement at a municipal special company. It sent the email to the company, which was the person's employer, and asked for a report on the employee. The employer opened disciplinary proceedings and dismissed the person. The Garante found there was no suitable legal basis and that purpose limitation and data minimisation were breached. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ended.

The Polish data protection authority was investigating complaints about two websites that processed data of professionals and did not identify the controller. It asked the sole trader behind them for information, including a further request on 15 April 2026, and he did not cooperate. The President of UODO opened separate proceedings and found that he breached Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR by not giving the authority access to the information it needed. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 7,500, set in the decision as PLN 31,507. The authority treated the breach as serious and found no mitigating factors.
The DPA fined a company PLN 31,507 (€7,200) for the failure to provide the DPA access to personal data and other information necessary for the performance of its tasks.

The Romanian DPA imposed a RON 26,236.50 (€5,000) fine on a cosmetics retailer for infringing Article 32 GDPR by failing to implement adequate security measures, after a cyberattack affecting its IT infrastructure led to a personal data breach.

After a cyber attack on its IT infrastructure led to unauthorised access to or disclosure of identification and contact data, the controller notified a personal data breach to the Romanian authority. The investigation, completed in July 2026, found it lacked appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It was fined RON 26,236.50 (about EUR 5,000) and ordered to implement access monitoring and logging with at least 30 days of log retention, including backup of the logs.

The DPC inquired into the HSE after two breaches in which intruders accessed paper medical records stored in disused, hazardous hospital buildings, and after a third unauthorised access to a basement. Twelve site inspections found records stored in neglected, damaged and insecure conditions. The DPC found infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 5(1)(e), 32(1), 33(1) and 34(1) GDPR. It reprimanded the HSE, ordered audits and remediation of storage facilities, and fined it a total of €645,000.
The DPA fined Uber €824.99 million for automatically deactivating drivers’ accounts without human intervention, in violation of Article 22 GDPR, and for insufficient transparency.

The Romanian DPA imposed a fine of RON 15,728 (€3,000) on a car dealer for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in order to guarantee the security of its processing, in breach of Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA fined a controller PLN 29,112 (€6,700) for a failure to comply with its previous decision ordering the controller to fulfil its information obligations under Article 14 GDPR. When determining the amount of the fine, the DPA took into account that the affected data subject remained in a state of uncertainty.

A complainant, an influencer, said Lab Pharma AS kept using her name and photos in its marketing after her 2016 agreement expired. The Norwegian authority, as lead authority in a cross-border case, found the processing had no legal basis. It ordered erasure and a stop to the use. It also fined the company NOK 205,000 for breaching the duty to cooperate with the authority (Art. 31). The company had resisted an information order, sent many hostile emails and delayed submitting the agreement. The fine was based on the turnover of Lab Pharma and a related company treated as one undertaking.

The DPA reprimanded a criminal records office for failing to implement appropriate security measures, including effective patch management and security monitoring, resulting in prolonged unauthorised access to systems containing sensitive personal data.

The DPA reprimanded a real estate agency for systematically storing all personal data contained in rental housing applications for 12 years in violation of the principles of storage limitation and data minimisation.

A security-guard employee complained to the Garante that his employer, La Patria S.p.A., had not answered two access requests made in June 2022 during a disciplinary procedure, and had raised other concerns about GPS devices on company cars. The Garante found that the company failed to answer the access requests properly, gave no proper notice about GPS geolocation of company vehicles, and gave employees notices that wrongly listed special categories of data. It dropped the other alleged breaches (Arts 5(1)(a), 6, 88 GDPR and Arts 113 and 114 of the Code). It fined the company EUR 39,000 in total, made up of EUR 22,000 for the access breach and the rest for the information breach, and ordered publication. No further corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ceased.

The DPA reprimanded an anti-doping organisation for publishing information on an athlete’s anti-doping infringement without a legal basis and held that the publication was a disproportionately severe measure with respect to the data subject’s right to privacy.

The DPA held that a pension insurance company lawfully disclosed a disability pension applicant's accrued pension to a physician tasked with evaluating the applicant's ability to work. According to the DPA, disclosing this information was appropriate and necessary.

The DPA fined a home and furniture retailer RON 78,570 (€15,000) after a cyberattack exploited an outdated website platform and weak passwords. It also imposed a RON 30,000 (€5,715) fine for placing non-essential cookies without consent.

After a personal data breach notification from HOMELUX S.R.L., the Romanian authority investigated and found that a cyberattack hit the website platform, which was not running the manufacturer's official version, and that weak passwords at account creation, left unfixed after the incident, made it easier. It found a breach of the security obligations in Art. 32 GDPR and of Art. 4(5) of Law 506/2004 because non-essential cookies were stored without user consent. The controller was fined RON 78,570 (EUR 15,000) under the GDPR and RON 30,000 under Law 506/2004. It was also ordered to put in place regular testing of systems, access and password security measures, protection of the web application, and cookie consent compliance.

The DPA fined a court bailiff PLN 15,500 (€3,500) for a failure to communicate the contact details of its data protection officer to the DPA. The DPA also found that the data protection officer had a conflict of interests with their other tasks and duties.

In March 2025 ransomware attacks hit on-premises servers and databases run by EETAA, the processor for the Ministry of Social Cohesion and Family's nursery-voucher programme and the 'Neighbourhood Nannies' pilot. The databases were encrypted and possibly exfiltrated, affecting roughly 2.5 million data subjects. After a hearing, the Authority fined the Ministry EUR 150,000 for infringing Article 5(1)(f) with Article 32(1) and EUR 50,000 for Article 28(3). It fined EETAA EUR 100,000 for Article 32(1) and EUR 50,000 for Article 28(3). It also ordered both to conclude a proper Article 28 contract within one month, and ordered EETAA to implement the planned security measures set out in the confidential annex within one month.

The DPA fined the controller €200,000 and the processor €150,000, after a large-scale data breach affecting 2,500,700 data subjects occurred due to outdated information systems, and inadequate security measures.

A former municipal employee complained that, after he returned from a long sick leave, the Municipality had changed the password of his PC and accessed his work email account. The Municipality said it acted urgently, after consulting its DPO, to ensure payroll and tax duties and avoid liability, and that it read only institutional emails. The Garante found the processing unlawful: no adequate legal basis, no respect for fairness and transparency, and a failure to apply data protection by design. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000 and ordered publication, with no further corrective measures because the conduct had ended and preventive measures were in place.

The Italian DPA has imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 on the Ancel Keys Comprehensive School in Castelnuovo Cilento. The complainant's child is enrolled at the nursery school run by the controller. The parent received a formal notice excluding their child from enrolment at the nursery school due to compulsory vaccination requirements. This information was also given to the mayor of the municipality, who informed the complainant's spouse about their child's exclusion. Information about data subjects' vaccination status is health data and therefore a category of special personal data. Although the school believed that they had informed the mayor of this information in their capacity as a local health authority, there was no legal basis for disclosing the data subjects' personal data to them.

A candidate complained that the Emilia-Romagna regional employment agency refused to delete her name from a published ranking list for hiring hospital reception technicians under Law 56/1987, which was also indexed by search engines. The Garante found no legal basis for publishing online the names of about 700 people enrolled in employment-centre lists, since the transparency rules the agency relied on (Art. 19 of Legislative Decree 33/2013) apply only to competitive recruitment procedures. It found breaches of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-septies(8) of the Code. It imposed a EUR 30,000 fine and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the agency had already removed and de-indexed the document.

The Italian DPA inspected TIM after numerous complaints about unsolicited promotional calls made by abusive call centres and sales agencies, often to numbers on the Public Opposition Register, using spoofed numbers and fake web 'leads'. It found that TIM's data-protection-by-design measures, supervision of its sales network and processors, security measures and handling of data subject rights were inadequate. The Authority declared the processing unlawful, ordered corrective measures on lead re-contact, partner oversight and data subject rights, and fined TIM EUR 9,516,000, about 1.7% of the statutory maximum. Two files were closed.

Two former employees complained that their individual company email accounts stayed active after their employment ended, with incoming mail redirected to another account, and that they had no proper privacy notice. The company argued the accounts were mere placeholders and had been deleted. The Garante found that forwarding continued for about 8 months (until October 2020) with no lawful basis, and that the privacy notices were outdated and inadequate. It found breaches of the lawfulness, minimisation and storage limitation principles and of Article 13, and fined the company EUR 6,500. It also invited the company to revise its new internal policy, and rejected the argument that the 120-day procedural deadline had expired.

A complainant reported that the Bologna University Hospital published on its website a PDF list of suitable and unsuitable candidates from an employment-centre hiring procedure, which was indexed by search engines. The list named about 95 participants, and mere participation could suggest a disability or unfavourable economic situation. The Garante found no legal basis for online publication and breaches of lawfulness and minimisation, and the hospital's reliance on transparency law (Art. 19 of Legislative Decree 33/2013) was rejected. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the order. No corrective measures were needed as the data had been removed.

An employee of the Ministry (ATA staff) complained that after she was dismissed in a disciplinary procedure, the disciplinary office of the Monza and Brianza territorial office emailed her name, identifying data and the dismissal to all regional school offices, all state schools in the area and several internal offices. The Garante found no legal basis for this wide disclosure, since sector rules only require candidates to self-declare and allow checks, and the recipients were third parties who did not need to know. Simply stating that the employment had ended would have sufficed. It declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, with publication of the order.
The DPA issued a warning against a media company for airing a deepfake of a known journalist without sufficiently marking the footage as AI-generated, in violation of Article 5(1)(a) and 25 GDPR.

The DPA fined an online store HUF 2,000,000 (€5,500) for a failure to provide customers concise, transparent, and intelligible information about the processing of their personal data; in particular, regarding the legal basis of the processing and data transfers to the United States.

The DPA held that a comparison platform for loans and financial products could request a customer to provide their residential address, personal identification number, and to sign their request electronically to verify the customer’s identity before fulfilling their access request.

The DPA fined a consulting firm €300,000 for failing to properly handle erasure requests and to inform data subjects of the outcome of their requests. The requests were related to the recruitment activities of the controller.

In summer 2025 an attacker used a single user account to enter the hospital's computerised patient summary and accessed data of 524,867 patients and 202,246 trusted third parties. The CNIL's restricted committee found that authentication was weak (no VPN or multifactor authentication), access control was too broad, and there was no real-time detection of suspicious activity. It also found that the trusted third parties were never directly informed of the breach. It fined the hospital EUR 500,000 and ordered completion of security measures within 3 to 15 months.

The DPA held that a city council violated Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(f) and 31 GDPR by publishing financial and sensitive data of applicants for social housing and failing to answer two information requests of the DPA.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation into Orange România SA in June 2026, started after the company notified a personal data breach. A mobile app flaw, caused by a synchronisation error between two interconnected applications, let one customer view and download other customers' equipment invoices. Separately, a publicly exposed ticketing platform with no VPN, MFA or IP restriction, and without regular security testing, allowed a cyber-attack and theft of a very large volume of personal data. The authority imposed two fines totalling RON 523,900 (about EUR 100,000), for Art. 25(1) (EUR 20,000) and Art. 32 (EUR 80,000), and ordered a monitoring and testing process for all IT applications.

An engineering consultancy was hit by a BlackBasta ransomware attack in October 2024. Files were encrypted and exfiltrated, the backup system was also affected, and part of the data was published on the dark web. The data included employee data, special categories (health, trade union membership) and training certificates of clients' employees, affecting more than 500 people. The Garante found that the company had not ensured adequate security of processing and breached Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 120,000 and ordered publication, with no further corrective measures because the company had improved its security afterwards.

The Municipality of Rieti mistakenly published on its official notice board and transparency section a determination with annexes, including the TARI (waste tax) roll of about 31,000 taxpayers with tax codes, names, addresses and cadastral data. The error was caused by a software default that publishes attachments, and the Municipality notified a breach and removed the documents after about 11 days. The Garante found breaches of the principles of lawfulness, minimisation, integrity and confidentiality, accountability, data protection by design and default, security, transparency and communication of the breach to data subjects. It fined the Municipality EUR 6,000, taking into account the medium gravity, negligence, small size, no prior violations and cooperation, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed as the conduct had ended.

The Italian DPA has imposed a fine of EUR 700 on La Terrazza. The controller installed a surveillance camera at their commercial premises. The camera captured part of the public space. Furthermore, the controller did not inform those affected by the camera of their rights regarding the processing of their personal data. The information provided listed a former business as the controller.

The DPA fined a subscription-based B2B contact-data platform €2,000,000 for processing professional contact data without a valid legal basis, in breach of transparency and minimisation requirements and for failing to implement privacy-by-design measures to exclude public officials’ data.

A public hospital in Thessaloniki mistakenly published on its website a weekly surgery list that still contained patients' phone numbers, conditions and scheduled operations, covering about 2,820 patients. The file stayed findable through Google from May to at least 29 August 2024 and was only noticed after a citizen reported it. The Authority found that security measures were inadequate (no second-person check, automation or test posting), that the breach was notified to it late (about 96 hours), that patients were not informed, and that the DPO's contact details were not published. It imposed four separate fines totalling EUR 25,000.

Several people were refused energy supply by Hera Comm and EstEnergy because of a poor risk score produced by the 'CGS-X' software, which combined an 'ESX score' from Experian Italia's credit information system with a Cerved score. When they made access requests, Experian only gave them the credit-register data and not the ESX score or sub-scores, and it generated a score even for people not in the register (based on residence address). After inspections of Experian, Hera, Major 1 and Cerved, the Garante found breaches of the principles of fairness/transparency and data minimisation, of the transparency and access-right provisions, and of data protection by design and by default. It ordered corrective measures (updated access-reply template, policy revision, rectification procedure, trimming of the XML data sent to Major 1) and fined Experian EUR 120,000.

The Italian DPA has imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 on Giuliano Isontina University Health Authority. The controller notified the relevant authorities of a personal data breach regarding a data subject's health record. The data subject's former spouse and three other healthcare professionals employed by the controller accessed this data without authorisation. The personal data could be accessed due to a loophole that allowed unauthorised personnel to access personal data via an override using a self-declaration form stating the reason for accessing that data.

The Garante learned from a report that the University of Pisa's exam registration portal let logged-in students see other students' data and cancel their exam registrations. The cause was an API update that returned an empty student-number field, which wrongly linked users' operations. 137 students and 221 registrations were affected, 156 of which were cancelled and later restored. The Garante found a disclosure without a legal basis and inadequate technical and organisational measures. It fined the University EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the order.

The Garante investigated Hera Comm S.p.A. after several people were refused energy supply because of a credit risk score ("Score CGS-X") built from Experian and Cerved data, although those providers held no negative information on them. After inspections at Hera, Major 1, Cerved and Experian, the Garante found breaches of the processing principles (lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, accuracy, storage limitation), of transparency and data subject rights (Arts. 12-15) and of Art. 28. It ordered Hera Comm to adopt a new access-reply model covering the score and its logic, send it to the complainants, and set up a rectification procedure with human intervention safeguards. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,800,000 and ordered publication.

Several people were refused an energy supply because of a risk score ("Score CGS-X") computed within the Hera Group from credit-information and commercial-information databases, even though those databases held no negative information about them. The Garante opened an own-initiative investigation with inspections at Hera, Major 1, Cerved and Experian, then examined EstEnergy. It found the processing unlawful: breaches of the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency, purpose limitation, accuracy and storage limitation, of the transparency and data subject rights provisions, and of the processor rules. It ordered EstEnergy to adopt a new Article 15 access reply model, send it to four complainants, and set up a rectification procedure with human intervention, within six months. It fined EstEnergy EUR 1,400,000 and ordered publication.

Several people were refused energy supply by Hera Comm and EstEnergy because of a risk score (CGS-X) that combined a Cerved score with an Experian score. When they made access requests, Cerved said it held no negative information on them and did not disclose the 'Score Retail Utilities' and sub-scores it had generated, because its complaints office could not technically see them. The Garante inspected the companies and found 2,094 data subjects affected over about two and a half years. It declared the processing unlawful for breach of Articles 5(1)(a), 12 and 15 GDPR, ordered a procedure to ensure the right to rectification of inaccurate scores, and fined Cerved EUR 400,000. Cerved had already introduced a dashboard and a new reply template.

A woman complained about an article in Il Fatto Quotidiano on a 2021 cable car accident. It named her and gave detailed information about her hospital stay, although she was only a witness in the criminal case. The publisher de-indexed the article and later removed it, but argued it had acted lawfully. The Garante found that naming her and the detailed health account breached the principles of lawfulness, fairness and minimisation and the essentiality of information rule. It fined the publisher EUR 23,750 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA opened an own-initiative investigation in November 2024 into the generative AI chatbot service Character.AI, offered in Italy by a US company. It found that the privacy policies were unclear and incomplete, that Italian data subjects were not properly informed about pre-training of the models, that age verification measures were inadequate for a period, that the DPIA was adopted late and that the EU representative was designated late. The Authority declared the processing unlawful, ordered the company to comply within 120 days and imposed a fine of EUR 158,000. Alleged breaches of Article 21 and Article 27(4) were not upheld.

The Italian DPA has imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 on the Municipality of San Genesio and Uniti. The data subject, a former employee of the municipality, stated in their complaint that, during the process of requesting a transfer of employment to another public body, the controller had revealed special categories of personal data, including their trade union membership. The controller did not have a legal basis for sharing those details; however, only one instance of such a breach is known.

The Italian DPA has imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 on the Municipality of Villaputzu. The data subject is a former employee of the municipality and controller. On the controllers website, a decision was published containing the data subjects personal data namely their registration number and the reason for the termination of their employment.

The DPA reprimanded the national police authority for not providing arriving travellers sufficient information regarding the processing of personal data that takes place during border control at an airport.

Romania's data protection authority concluded an investigation into Banca Transilvania S.A. in June 2026 after a complaint from a customer. A bank employee, at a third party's request and outside their duties, accessed the complainant's account statements without authorisation. The authority found the bank had not put in place adequate technical and organisational security measures, in breach of Article 32(1), (2) and (4) GDPR. It fined the bank 26,172 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to implement measures preventing employees from accessing personal data for personal interest. The bank has already paid the fine.

The Romanian DPA, acting as lead authority after a referral from the French CNIL, investigated Ascendex Technology SRL over an erasure request. The company took about 12 months to handle the complainant's request, never sent a final reply and did not justify the delay; for other data subjects the delay reached 37 months. The authority found breaches of Articles 12(1) and (3) read with Article 17(1) GDPR and fined the company 57,839 lei (about EUR 11,000). It also ordered the company to reply properly to the complainant and similar data subjects and to train staff regularly on handling data subject requests.

The DPA held that an employee’s complaint alleging that their employer monitored her work and allowed colleagues to access her personal files was unsubstantiated. The DPA considered that the employer had implemented appropriate security measures such as access controls.
The DPA reprimanded a school in Reykjavik, after they received an anonymous tip about the data subject, for unlawfully processing without a legal basis personal data.

A private website operator published documents they collected from public registers. The DPA held that the operator failed to ensure that later access restrictions imposed by the authorities are considered and that a legitimate interest could not be a blanket legal basis for all publications.

The DPA fined a medical company €450,000 after a third party had gained access to the health data of patients due to the controller’s failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures resulting in a violation of the principles of integrity and confidentiality.

Following petitions from an individual, the Romanian authority investigated Altex România and found that a technical vulnerability in its mobile app's account validation let a user access another person's name, invoices and delivery addresses. The company had not implemented adequate security measures, did not notify the authority of the breach and did not inform the affected person. It was fined separately under Articles 32, 33 and 34 (7,000 + 2,000 + 1,000 EUR equivalent, 10,000 in total) and ordered to take corrective measures including reviewing authentication, testing for vulnerabilities, incident procedures, staff training and replying to the complainant.

A former agency worker complained that his employer's user company, Cosmint, opened his personal locker in his absence after his contract ended and threw away its contents. Cosmint also failed to answer the Garante's request for information. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness, fairness, transparency and minimisation principles, the legal basis rules and the information duty, plus Article 157 of the Italian Code. It rejected Cosmint's arguments that the GDPR did not apply and that the breach was minor. It imposed a fine of EUR 6,600 and ordered publication.

A complainant said the Enna health authority published a resolution online with an attachment containing his judicial data, and did not properly act on his erasure request. The authority had hidden the data in one section but they stayed visible, by mistake, in another section of its website until the Garante's inquiry. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5, 6, 10 and 17 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-octies of the Code. It fined the authority EUR 20,000, giving decisive weight to earlier similar violations, and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended.

The Italian DPA has imposed a fine of EUR 2,075 on Edizione Grandangolo di Giuseppe Castaldo. The data subject filed a complaint stating that even after requesting the deletion of their personal data their name and images remained accessible in an online news publication. The publication had published this personal data while the data subject was still a minor. The subsequent investigation found that the publication had been the victim of a cyber attack due to inadequate technical security measures, a fact which it had not reported to the relevant authority. The publication also lacked a privacy policy.

Many healthcare clinics notified the Garante of a ransomware attack on servers of the GIPO division of Docplanner Italy, which manages clinic management software as processor. After inspections, the Garante found that the company's security measures were inadequate: outdated security equipment, weak access security (no multi-factor authentication for some accounts) and insufficient detection of breaches. It found violations of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR and fined the company EUR 10,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the company had since strengthened its security. The decision is to be published.

The Italian DPA has imposed a fine of EUR 90,000 on Acquirente Unico S.p.A. Acquirente Unico manages an integrated information system comprising a database of energy delivery points for gas and electricity as well as identifying and contractual data on end customers. A data subject filed a request to update their personal data regarding a gas supply identifier that had been attributed to a deceased person. The controller did not comply with the request, stating that they were not responsible for communication between end customers and energy suppliers. Investigators found that in three specific cases the database contained supply contracts linked to deceased individuals. Furthermore investigators found that there were 11,711 customers over 100 years old with 25,713 active supply contracts in their name.

The DPA fined Piaggio €460,000 after finding that its long-term retention and examination of employees’ emails and logs enabled unlawful workplace monitoring and that it had failed to respond to account deactivation requests.
The DPA reprimanded a security services company for installing cameras in its patrol vehicles and recording its drivers without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR.

The DPA fined an accounting and tax consulting company €2,760 for a failure to implement technical and organisational measures following a data breach that lead to unauthorised access to personal data processed via email.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in May 2026 into the Romanian National Post Company, acting as a processor. The investigation began after a social assistance directorate reported that mail sent through the post company never reached recipients. The authority found that the post company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures, leading to loss or destruction of postal items containing personal data of many people. It fined the company 26,026 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to review and update its technical and organisational measures and working procedures.

A person complained about two companies, MEDE S.A. and Market In AEBE, over their video surveillance systems. He said his access request was not properly answered and that footage was passed to third parties. The Authority found that MEDE S.A. disclosed footage to judicial authorities without properly informing the data subject, which breached the transparency and purpose-limitation principles and Article 13. It also found that MEDE S.A. did not facilitate or satisfy the access request and did not notify its data protection officer's contact details to the Authority. It fined MEDE S.A. EUR 65,000 in total, in four separate fines. It fined Market In AEBE separately (EUR 95,000 in total); that part is not detailed here.

A complainant lodged complaints against two companies, MEDE AE and Market In AEBE, over their CCTV systems. He said his access request was not properly met, that CCTV images were processed unlawfully, and that they were disclosed to third parties without informing him. The Authority found that Market In disclosed CCTV photos to the judicial authorities without properly informing the data subject, breached data minimisation and accountability, failed to satisfy the access request (Arts 12 and 15), and did not cooperate with the Authority (Art. 31). It fined Market In a total of EUR 95,000 across four separate fines. MEDE AE was also fined, in the same decision, for its own infringements.

The DPA fined the operator of an exhibition centre and a supermarket chain €65,000 and €95,000 respectively for failures relating to the disclosure and further use of CCTV footage, responses to access requests and compliance with multiple data-protection principles and obligations.

The DPC announced its final decision on an inquiry into a ransomware attack on the laboratory information system at Midlands Regional Hospital Tullamore, detected in November 2018. The attackers encrypted patients' personal data, and about 84,000 people were estimated to be affected. The DPC found that the HSE infringed Articles 5(1)(f), 28, 30, 32(1) and 34 GDPR. It reprimanded the HSE, fined it EUR 300,000 for the Article 5(1)(f) and 32(1) infringements, and ordered it to implement specified security policies and procedures.

A person whose number was in the Public Opposition Register complained about an unsolicited marketing call and email made by Green Partner, a sales agency of the energy company Sorgenia, and about an inadequate reply to their rights request. Green Partner first disowned the call, then said it was a mistyped number dialled by a sub-contracted call-centre worker. The Garante found processing without a valid legal basis, an unclear processor role and processor duties breached for years, and inadequate handling of data subject rights. It ordered corrective measures on use of sub-processors and fined the company EUR 15,300, with publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA received a report from the Carabinieri health unit, which found during judicial checks that the Lecce local health authority could not show any formal appointment of authorised staff or written instructions in its urology ward. Patient records were kept in an unlocked trolley, an unauthorised person had shadowed ward staff with a doctor's complicity, and none of the 44 ward employees had attended data protection training. The Garante found breaches of the integrity and confidentiality and accountability principles and of Articles 29 and 32, and fined the authority EUR 4,500 and ordered publication of the decision.
The DPA reprimanded a hospital and its email service provider for a failure to implement technical and organisational measures following a data breach that involved health data of patients.

The DPA fined a provider of a hospital €300,000 for inadequate security measures which enabled a ransomware attack affecting health data of 84,000 people, alongside violations of Articles 28, 30 and 34 GDPR.
The DPA fined a medical services employee €1,200 for photographing two patients and sharing the images with unauthorised third parties because they contained health data under Article 9(1) GDPR.

The DPA held that a convicted data subject could not demand the operator of a search engine to delist a URL linking to their convictions because of the nature of the convictions as recent and particularly serious.

The DPA fined a municipality €5,000 for not providing data subjects with sufficient information relating to the cameras used to record driving violations. The municipality also processed an excessive amount of data by not limiting the image to the data subject’s license plate.

The DPA fined a doctor €1,153 for unlawfully accessing the data of over 1,200 patients of a medical centre the doctor worked for. Acting as a controller, the doctor invited the patients to a new medical institution they planned to move to.

A customer complained about two bodies: an energy supplier (ZeniΘ) and Piraeus Bank. Electricity bills were being paid by direct debit from a joint bank account without his consent, and neither would give him copies of the signed direct debit mandates. The Authority found several infringements by the supplier and fined it EUR 25,000 + 25,000 + 50,000. As to the Bank, it found a minor breach of the accuracy principle (Art. 5(1)(d)), for which it issued a reprimand, and a breach of the right of access (Art. 15), for which it fined the Bank EUR 10,000. Mitigating: the Bank gave some information and contacted another bank to try to solve the issue.

The DPA fined an energy provider €100,000 and a bank €10,000 over a customer’s disputed direct debit mandates. Both controllers failed to properly respond to his access requests and breached the accuracy principle, while the energy provider also failed to control its processor.

The President of the Polish data protection authority fined the Minister of Justice PLN 100,000 over the 2019 'hater affair'. Public officials in the Ministry used judges' personal data from confidential personnel files for personal and political purposes and passed it to unauthorised people, including journalists, and posted it online. The authority found that the Minister had not put in place suitable security measures and had not supervised the authorisations given to staff. Special category data (health, political views, affiliations) were involved. The authority treated the fact that the offender was a constitutional state body as aggravating. This text is a news item about the decision, not the decision itself.

The Authority examined twelve complaints from subscribers about calls made on behalf of the energy company PPC (ΔΕΗ). The calls were made by PPC's partner call centres, including MEDIATEL, TP, CQS and PRELUDE. It found failures in security measures (Art. 32 GDPR), in compliance with the Art. 11 of Law 3471/2006 opt-out register, and in Art. 5 GDPR, and fined PPC and the four call-centre companies. MEDIATEL was fined EUR 45,000 for Art. 32 GDPR and EUR 55,000 for Art. 11 of Law 3471/2006. It was also ordered to improve its procedures technically within six months.

The Authority examined twelve complaints from telephone subscribers about promotional or survey calls made on behalf of the energy company PPC (DEH) by outsourced call centres. It grouped the cases and found infringements by PPC and by its processors. TP, one of the call centres, was fined EUR 50,000 for breach of Article 32 GDPR (security of processing) and EUR 40,000 for breach of Article 5 GDPR. It was also ordered to improve its technical procedures within six months so that such failures cannot recur. The Authority rated the gravity of the infringements as low and accepted gradual improvement of compliance measures as mitigating.

The Authority examined twelve complaints from telephone subscribers about unsolicited calls made for the energy company PPC. The calls were made by PPC's partner call centres. It decided jointly on PPC and four call-centre companies: CQS, TP, MEDIATEL and PRELUDE. PRELUDE was found to have breached Article 32 GDPR (security of processing) and Articles 28 and 29 GDPR (processor obligations). It was fined EUR 50,000 and EUR 30,000 for these, EUR 80,000 in total, and ordered to improve its technical procedures within six months. The detailed reasoning for PRELUDE (section 12e) is not in the excerpt.

The Authority examined twelve complaints from subscribers about telephone calls made on behalf of the energy supplier PPC (DEI) by its partner call centres. The calls were made by PPC's processors CQS, TP, MEDIATEL and PRELUDE. In a single decision it fined PPC and the four call-centre companies for failures under Articles 32 and 5 GDPR, Articles 28 and 29 GDPR (PRELUDE only) and Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 (the Article 11 do-not-call register). CQS was fined EUR 20,000 for the Article 32 GDPR breach and EUR 40,000 for the Article 11 breach, and was ordered to improve its technical procedures within six months.

The DPA fined an energy supplier and four call-centre operators €880,000 in total for inadequate technical and organisational measures, mixed-purpose calls, insufficient processor oversight and unauthorised use of a subcontractor.

Following an on-site inspection in June 2022, the Norwegian DPA found that Elkjøp's customer club consent was invalid (not informed, specific or freely given). It also found that the 'kundematch' tool lacked a legal basis and no compatibility assessment, that the use of offline conversions was not adequately assessed or documented, and that data subject requests were handled outside the Article 12(3) deadlines. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 20,000,000 on Elkjøp Nordic AS and Elkjøp Norge AS. The fine was set far below the EDPB starting range, mainly because of the long case processing time and the improvements made after the inspection.
The DPA reprimanded a company for refusing to cooperate with the DPA, since the controller had failed to provide information on the processing of personal data in two pending cases against it.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into Unicredit Bank SA after a petition from an individual. The bank sent erroneous insurance policy expiry notifications to a large number of customers, disclosing other customers' data because of a file-processing error with improper manual handling. The authority found failures in technical and organisational security measures and a late breach notification beyond 72 hours. It imposed two fines totalling 62,714 lei (EUR 12,000 equivalent): EUR 10,000 equivalent for Article 32 and EUR 2,000 equivalent for Article 33.
The DPA fined a news website HUF 25,000,000 (approximately €70,590) for unlawfully publishing the personal data of a data subject in articles related to court proceedings they were involved in.
The EDPB held that an organised and standardised complaint strategy does not, in itself, constitute an abuse of rights and instructed the Belgian DPA to assess the complaint on its merits.

A driver employed by a Ligurian health authority complained that he was suspended after a disciplinary procedure based on satellite tracking data from a company vehicle. Other employees raised similar complaints, and the Garante examined them together. It found that the vehicle geolocation produced almost continuous monitoring of employees and that the data were used for disciplinary purposes, in breach of the GDPR principles, legal basis, data protection by design, DPIA and employment-context rules. Because the authority had since lengthened the tracking interval from 60 seconds to 15 minutes and permanently disabled real-time tracking, no further corrective measures were ordered. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 6,000, with publication.

A former employee complained that the Municipality of Sciacca published on its website a managerial determination recording their voluntary resignation and the calculation of the notice-period indemnity, with their name in the title. The Garante found that no law required this publication, so there was no valid legal basis and the data minimisation and lawfulness principles were breached. The Municipality had already redacted the data after the proceedings began, so no corrective measures were ordered. The Garante fined the Municipality EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the injunction on its website.
The DPA fined the Italian Red Cross €700 for unlawfully disclosing a hospitalised patient’s medical condition along with their full name in a note next to the patient’s meal tray.
The DPA fined the government agency for digitalization €55,000 for failing to inform data subjects about the inclusion of their certified email addresses in a public index of registered addresses.

The CNIL restricted committee sanctioned IQVIA Operations France, which runs two authorised health data warehouses (LRX from pharmacies and EMR from doctors). Following a TV report, complaints and inspections in 2021, it found breaches of Article 66 of the French Data Protection Act and of Articles 14 and 25 GDPR. It imposed a EUR 5,000,000 fine, calculated using the turnover of the US parent company as part of the same economic unit. It also ordered compliance measures with a EUR 10,000 per day penalty after six months, and ordered publication, with the company no longer named after two years.

The DPA fined a controller PLN 21,000 (€4,900) and a processor PLN 12,500 (€2,900) following a data breach due to a failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and insufficient processor oversight.

In an earlier decision of 21 October 2025 the Polish DPA ordered a private individual to stop recording the image and voice of his neighbours with a video surveillance system that reached beyond his property. A follow-up check found that he never showed he had complied, and the neighbours said the monitoring went on. The DPA opened proceedings on its own initiative and found that he breached Article 58(2)(d) GDPR by not complying with the order. It imposed a fine of PLN 26,711 under Article 83(6). He had not given his income data, so the fine was estimated at three times the average monthly wage. The decision is marked as not yet final.
The DPA fined an individual PLN 26,711 (approximately €6,174) for refusing to comply with an earlier decision stating their camera surveillance beyond their property was unlawful.
The DPA fined a company £300,000 (€ 348,478.5) for sending over 5.5 million unsolicited direct marketing SMS without valid consent and concealing its identity.

The Polish data protection authority opened proceedings on its own initiative against a social welfare centre. It found that the centre had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data, had not notified the supervisory authority of a personal data breach, and had not informed the affected individuals. It imposed three separate fines of PLN 15,000, PLN 5,500 and PLN 13,200, within the PLN 100,000 cap for public budgetary units. It also ordered the centre to notify the affected people of the breach within 7 days of delivery of the decision.

The DPA imposed three separate fines amounting to PLN 33,700 (€7,800) on a municipal social welfare unit for multiple GDPR violations, including a failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and to notify a data breach that involved health data of customers.
The DPA reprimanded a mayor for the unlawful disclosure of a data subject’s name and email address to multiple recipients in connection with a request for access to public information.

The DPA found that a company providing AI powered reports of the “online presence” of data subjects failed to provide a data subject with access to their data, and ordered it to comply with the access request.
The DPA fined a marketing company €1,500 for unlawfully sending unsolicited communications in the context of a B2B marketing campaign.

A passenger with reduced mobility complained that Emirates required her to fill in the MEDIF medical form and send health information without any privacy notice or information on how the data would be processed. The Garante investigated and found that Emirates' information to passengers was inadequate and that the seven-year retention of MEDIF forms breached the storage limitation principle. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and (e), 12 and 13 GDPR and fined Emirates EUR 180,000. It also ordered Emirates to clarify which categories of passengers must complete the form and which fields are needed, and to set specific retention periods and delete data beyond them within 30 days.

The municipality of Ventasso published online the list of candidates admitted to the written test of a recruitment procedure reserved for protected categories (disabled persons) under Law 68/1999. The list revealed indirectly health data of 12 people and stayed online, then reachable via a direct link, for a long period. The Garante rejected the municipality's argument that the mountain union was the controller, finding the municipality was the controller and the union its processor. It found a breach of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-septies(8) of the Code, and fined the municipality EUR 8,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased once the list was removed.

A customer asked Lidl Italia by certified email, within hours of an incident at a store in Arco (TN), for access to the CCTV images of him and for their retention. Lidl insisted on its own request form and then deleted the footage, and replied by registered post, not the PEC the customer used. The reply also omitted the right to complain to the authority. The Garante found breaches of fairness, facilitation of rights, access and restriction, and fined Lidl EUR 43,000, also ordering publication of the order on its website.

A patient of a dental clinic complained that the clinic's operator gave incomplete privacy information and kept handwritten records. Vortika s.r.l. had taken over the clinic by leasing the business from the previous operator, which was in liquidation. The Garante found that Vortika never gave patients the Article 14 information, that the notice it later published wrongly relied on consent for treatment data and cited Article 10, and that it had not appointed a data protection officer although it processed health data on a large scale. It fined the company EUR 20,000 for the transparency breaches and EUR 10,000 for the missing DPO, EUR 30,000 in total, ordered corrective measures within 90 days and ordered publication. The handwritten-records issue was attributed to the previous operator.

The Garante investigated an energy supplier following one complaint and some thirty reports of unwanted telemarketing calls, many to numbers on the Public Opposition Register, made by partners and unregistered callers who pushed contracts with the company. It found the company processed data without a valid legal basis or proper information, failed to define roles and supervise its telemarketing partners, and answered a rights request inadequately. It ordered corrective measures covering the whole chain from contact to contract and the oversight of processors, and imposed a EUR 100,000 fine with publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA inspected a Naples hospital trust in January 2026 to check its electronic health dossier against the 2015 guidelines. It found the dossier was over-broadly accessible to doctors and nurses, consultation of records was not logged, consent for past data was not collected separately, the privacy notice did not match the real processing and no retention periods were set. The trust fixed most issues during the proceedings, so no corrective measures were ordered. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000, with publication of the decision.

The DPA investigated a workplace consulting company providing sentiment analyses of messages exchanged by employees in order to assess their stress level and prepare a respective report to their employer. The DPA issued a warning, stating its concern that, in the future, data subjects could unlawfully be identified by the reports.

The DPA rejected a foreign national’ s complaint seeking deletion from the National Registry of Undesirable Aliens, holding that his entry ban for national security reasons was lawful and classified data was properly withheld under GDPR.

The DPA fined a tech company a total of €176,946.61 for unlawfully keeping active the email account of a contractor after they left the company and for transparency obligation infringements. The DPA also ordered the company to comply with the contractor's access request, provide access logs, delete the personal data afterwards and take measures to ensure future compliance.

A complainant challenged the Walloon water utility SWDE over recording and listening to customer phone calls for quality control and staff training. The Litigation Chamber found infringements of the transparency and fairness rules (Articles 5(1)(a), 12 and 13) and of the processor-contract rules (Article 28(3)). It imposed two fines, EUR 85,000 for the transparency/fairness infringements and EUR 1,000 for the processor infringement, EUR 86,000 in total. Other infringements received reprimands and compliance orders. The fines were cut from EUR 120,000 and EUR 1,200 after the Chamber weighed mitigating factors, proportionality and the financial context. The decision has been appealed to the Market Court.

The DPA fined an operator of a digital authentication and identification service €120,000 for wrongly qualifying itself as a processor rather than a controller. It held that this breached the accountability principle and led to further infringements concerning transparency, the right of access, data minimisation and data protection by default.

The DPA fined the operator of an online store HUF 15,000,000 (€41,500) for not providing its customers concise, transparent, and intelligible information on the purposes, legal basis, and duration of processing and data transfers to third countries.

The DPA held that a doctor unlawfully accessed a data subject’s medical records without proving a valid legal basis, but took no corrective measure, considering that the doctor had provided some medical advice at the data subject’s request.

The DPA ordered the management of an apartment complex to verify if it had a legitimate interest to keep and operate surveillance cameras and reprimanded it for failing to inform residents, to respond to an access request and to have an agreement in place with a processor.

A mother and her minor daughter complained against a law firm that had represented the mother. The firm answered their access requests only partially, citing lack of proof of identity and then demanding EUR 135 as the requests were deemed manifestly unfounded or excessive. It had also not properly informed them about the processing of their data. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of the transparency principle and information duties and of the right of access. It imposed two fines (EUR 2,520 and EUR 2,400), ordered the firm to answer the access request within one month, and ordered publication.

The DPC announced its final decision on an inquiry into three personal data breaches at Permanent TSB. Malicious actors holding some customer information phoned the Open24 Contact Centre, posed as customers and changed account details. The DPC found infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1) and 33(1) GDPR, including late notification of the breaches. It reprimanded PTSB and imposed fines of EUR 250,000 and EUR 27,500, EUR 277,500 in total. The full decision is to be published later; this text is only a press release.

The DPA found that an insurance company had not provided a data subject with information required under Articles 14 GDPR within the statutory timeframe. However, the DPA considered that the data subject could not object to the company transferring data related to their debt to their processor, a debt collection agency.

A cyber-attack began in September 2020 with a phishing email. The attacker stayed dormant until May 2022, then moved through the network and stole data, and about 4 TB of it was published on the dark web. The ICO found that the water group did not have adequate security for its IT environment, in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) UK GDPR. The breach affected about 633,887 customers and employees. The ICO imposed a single penalty of £963,900, which already includes a reduction for a voluntary settlement. The companies admitted the infringements and agreed not to appeal.

A water supplier was fined £963,900 (€1,113,858.12) for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures enabling a successful phishing campaign resulting in a data breach and the publication of more than 600,000 data subjects’ data on the dark web.

The DPA held that an employer violated an employee’s right of access by refusing to provide copies of their timesheets and offering only an inspection on its premises. The DPA also found that the workload involved in fulfilling the access request was due to the controller’s own archiving system and not because the request was excessive.
The DPA fined a processor tasked with the maintenance of an online store €2,802 because of its failure to ensure the security of processing on the store.

The DPA fined a municipality PLN 7,700 (approximately €1,813) for not reporting a data breach to the DPA. The municipality mistakenly published a file with information of data subjects who signed a petition.

The Irish DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into PTSB after breach notifications concerning its Open24 Contact Centre, where customers suffered financial loss and fraud risk. It found infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1) and 33(1) GDPR. It imposed a reprimand and two fines: EUR 250,000 for Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1), and EUR 27,500 for Article 33(1), totalling EUR 277,500. The fines were lower than the EUR 385,000 proposed in the draft decision because of PTSB's mitigation and prompt improvements.

The DPA fined an online store operator HUF 10,000,000 (€27,300) as there was no privacy notice available on the store’s website. In particular, information on the purposes and the legal bases of processing, the storage periods, and the recipients of personal data was missing.

The Italian DPA inspected Lepida, an in-house public company that issues SPID digital identities (LepidaID), as part of a programme of checks on SPID providers. It found that about 7,000 counter operators could access personal data and copies of identity and health cards of all 1.5 million users, that documents were kept on counter workstations, that checks with external databases were done insecurely, that transaction logs were kept too long, and that the privacy notice misdescribed Lepida's role. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined Lepida EUR 100,000 and ordered publication. One charge, on the storage security of transaction tracking information, was closed, and no corrective measures were ordered because remedial steps had been taken.

The mother of a deceased infant complained that photos of her child, with clinical details, had been published in a congress e-poster on a paediatrics society website. The doctor who submitted the poster argued that the eyes were masked and the data were pseudonymised. The Garante held that masking the eyes is not anonymisation, the data were identifiable health data, and the father's consent (which referred only to anonymous communication) was not valid. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), (b), (c) and 9 GDPR and fined the doctor EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the poster had been removed.

A prison officer complained that a service order containing information on his health (physical condition, need to alternate posture, as prescribed by the occupational physician) was posted on notice boards in the Cosenza prison's staff areas and sent to various offices and trade unions. The Garante found that the Ministry of Justice, as controller, disclosed health data without a suitable legal basis, breaching Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 9 GDPR and section 2-ter of the Italian Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 12,000, treating the seriousness as medium, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

The Matera Local Health Authority notified the Garante of a ransomware attack by the Rhysida group that encrypted its servers and exfiltrated about 600 GB of data, affecting 95,362 people, including health data. After requests for information and an inspection, the Garante found that the Authority's security measures were insufficient (single-factor VPN access with broad privileges, limited network segmentation, outdated systems, and a SIEM that raised no alert on the attacker's logins). It found a breach of the integrity and confidentiality principle and of the security obligations. It fined the Authority EUR 8,600 and ordered publication of the decision.

A supermarket operator, acting as processor for a loyalty card scheme run by Conad Adriatico, used loyalty-card transaction data to bring a disciplinary charge against a cashier, which led to her dismissal. The cashier complained to the Garante, also because her rights request of 15 February 2023 got no reply. The Garante found breaches of the processing principles, lawfulness, transparency, data subject rights and processor rules (Art. 28(3)). It banned further processing of her loyalty-card data in the employment context and fined the company EUR 34,000, with the decision to be published.

The Italian DPA investigated an energy supplier after a complaint about two unsolicited promotional calls, the first by an outside agency acting for it, and about an inadequate reply to an access request. The company said the data came via an agency, which had obtained it from a lead-generation website, and that consent had been given. The Garante found processing without a valid legal basis, failure of accountability and processor oversight, and failure to handle the data subject's rights request and to have suitable procedures. It imposed a fine of EUR 15,000, ordered publication of the decision on its website and noted it in its internal register.

Following a complaint about a marketing SMS sent without consent, the Romanian authority investigated a gambling platform operator. It found that the operator collected the complainant's phone number when another person opened an online gaming account, without checking accuracy. It also found that the operator unlawfully and excessively collected and stored the complainant's ID copy and a selfie while handling his request. Two fines of EUR 20,000 and EUR 15,000 (total EUR 35,000) were imposed, plus two corrective orders on accuracy of data and data minimisation.
The DPA fined an NGO €1,000 for failing to cooperate with the DPA in accordance with Article 31 GDPR in course of a complaint procedure concerning a data subject’s erasure request.

The DPA fined a pharmaceutical consulting firm €5,000,000 for insufficiently anonymising data processed in its pharmacy and medical-record data warehouse, allowing the unwanted identification of data subjects by singling them out. The DPA ordered the controller to bring its processing into compliance.

A former employee complained that his employer kept his professional email address and mailbox active after the employment ended and did not respond to his erasure request. The Litigation Chamber found the continued processing unlawful, found erasure and transparency failings, and found accountability failings. It ordered the processing stopped and the email address and mailbox permanently deleted within 30 days. It reprimanded the company for the accountability breaches. It fined the company EUR 8,500 for the breach of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR, the only breach fined.

The DPA reprimanded a real estate agency for replying to a tenant’s access request over four years late, rejecting the argument that the mere existence of a dispute between the parties made the request manifestly unfounded or excessive.

The DPA found that a soccer club failed to respect a data subject’s objection and erasure request by continuing to send promotional emails even after the data subject clicked on the “unsubscribe” link.

The DPA fined a company €20,000 for failing to inform a former employee before disclosing emails containing her personal data to her former supervisor. It also fined the supervisor €2,000 as a separate controller for failing to inform her about his collection, retention and later disclosure of the emails for use in litigation.

The DPA found that a Catalan city council had infringed the principle of data minimisation by including unnecessary and excessive personal data in a mayoral decree initiating disciplinary proceedings against a local police officer.

A former employee complained that after his employment ended his individual company email accounts stayed active and his request to delete them received no reply within the deadline. The Garante found the company kept the accounts active for six months without adequately informing employees, did not answer the erasure request in time and had not given proper written instructions to the IT staff member handling the accounts. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered the company to prepare a proper privacy notice and give specific instructions to IT staff, and fined it EUR 5,000, taking into account that the company is in liquidation.

An employee of the municipality of Campo Calabro complained that a determination and its annexes, ranking staff for a pay-grade progression, were published on the online notice board with names and scores. The Garante found there was no legal basis for publishing this data, since the cited transparency rules do not require it and consent cannot serve as a basis in the public employment context. It found breaches of the lawfulness and minimisation principles and Article 6 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 6,000, with no corrective measures because the data had already been obscured, and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA fined the Italian Post and PostePay a total of €12,501,000 for multiple infringements relating to the processing of personal data for the detection of malware from the devices of users who installed the controllers’ applications.

The company notified the Garante of a data breach in which an attacker exfiltrated authentication credentials (usernames, passwords, email addresses) from its web training portals. The Garante found that passwords were weakly protected (MD5 hashing, in one case plaintext), that old credentials were kept far longer than needed, and that the data subjects were not informed in time. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(e) and (f), 32 and 34 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 85,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.
The DPA ordered a dental clinic to review its relationship with the provider of a specific dental treatment and remedy transparency and consent failures in connection to its patients’ treatment.
The DPA fined an insurance company €200,000 for failing to ensure security of processing, which allowed a former employee to access a data subject’s account.

The AEPD opened a sanction procedure against CaixaBank after two complaints, one concerning a personal data breach in its customer service department (SAC), where similar breaches occurred in 2023. The investigator proposed a EUR 500,000 fine for breaching Article 25 GDPR (data protection by design and by default) and the closure of the Article 5(1)(f) charge. CaixaBank paid voluntarily on 19 March 2026, without admitting liability, obtaining the 20% reduction to EUR 400,000. The AEPD's final resolution confirms the Article 25 infringement, archives the Article 5(1)(f) charge, ends the procedure and orders a review of how the SAC works.

The DPA fined a sub-processor €2,415 for a failure to implement technical and organisational measures to guarantee the security of processing: former employees of the sub-processor still had access to customers’ personal data that was shared on an app.
The DPA held that a bailiff cannot reject an Article 15 GDPR access request concerning personal data processed in enforcement proceedings without providing any explanation.

The DPA held that an employer lawfully disclosed the personal data of an employee, including information about trade union membership, to a third party advising the employer in the context of a labour dispute.

The DPA dismissed a complaint for lack of evidence. Additionally, it held that the cancellation of an insurance policy due to a human error had no significant societal or personal impact, even more so when the insurer reversed the decision at the request of the beneficiary’s representative.

The Dutch DPA fined MLU B.V., successor to the dissolved Ridetech International B.V., EUR 100 million. Ridetech operated the Yango ride-hailing app and transferred personal data of Finnish and Norwegian users and drivers to Yandex entities in Russia without showing appropriate safeguards. The AP found that Russia does not ensure an adequate level of protection and that data subjects lacked enforceable rights and effective remedies. The violation began on 23 May 2022 and is ongoing. Besides the fine, the AP imposed an immediate ban on transferring such data to recipients in Russia.

The DPA dismissed a customer's complaint claiming they received invoices addressed to other customers of the controller. The DPA held that it was impossible to verify the facts of the case, as the customer had destroyed all invoices.

The DPA reprimanded an insurance company for allowing to change the delivery address of e-invoices via unverified reference numbers alone. This lack of security measures resulted in a data subject receiving another data subject's e-invoices due to a simple typing error.

A former employee complained that Esselunga never replied in writing to his access request of 8 September 2024 for his attendance records from 1997 to 2024. The company only phoned him to ask the reasons for the request and gave a full reply on 10 December 2024, after the Garante invited it to comply. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR, rated the seriousness as medium, and fined the company EUR 5,000. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

Greenpeace Onlus reported that Eni published on its website, in full, the writ of summons in a climate lawsuit brought against it by Greenpeace, ReCommon and twelve citizens, without redacting the citizens' birth details, tax codes and home addresses. Eni argued legitimate interest, and said the data was largely already public and the publication incidental. The Garante found the processing unlawful for lack of a valid legal basis, contrary to Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 96,000, taking into account the negligent nature, the moderate duration (no more than about 6 months), the 12 data subjects, Eni's prompt removal of the data and its cooperation. No further corrective measures were ordered, since Eni had already stopped the processing. The order is to be published on the Garante's website.

The DPA fined a bank €31,800,000 for not implementing sufficient safeguards to prevent an employee from accessing the financial data of over 3,500 data subjects for non-service related purposes. The controller also failed to inform the DPA and the affected data subjects about the data breach on time.

The complainant, the municipality's secretary general, complained that the municipality published on its online notice board a council resolution and a payment decision revealing her pregnancy, maternity, parental leave and sick leave. The Garante found that publication, which continued in the 'historical' notice board section well beyond the legal 15 days, was a dissemination of personal and health data without a legal basis and breached the lawfulness and minimisation principles. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000, considering the breach negligent, medium in gravity, and the municipality small and cooperative. No further corrective measures were ordered because the data had been removed.

The DPA warned a region's Nature and Forests Department as well as the region's Economic, Social and Environmental Council for failing to respond in time to access requests submitted by a hunter following a hunting exemption application. In addition, the DPA warned the Council to comply with the hunter’s erasure request.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation into Renault Commercial Roumanie after the company notified a personal data breach. A cyberattack on an application run by a processor led to unauthorised access to and publication of many people's personal data on a platform. The authority found the controller had not put in place adequate security measures and had not ensured it used processors giving sufficient guarantees. It fined the company RON 637,262.50, equivalent to EUR 125,000.
