A company's representative secretly recorded a business conversation with two people without valid consent or other legal basis. The Austrian DPA upheld the data protection complaint, found a breach of the right to secrecy, and then fined the company EUR 6,300 in administrative penalty proceedings. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the company's appeal as unfounded and confirmed the penalty, holding the amount unobjectionable. It ordered the company to pay 20% of the fine (EUR 1,260) as appeal costs and held that a further appeal (Revision) is not admissible. The hearing went ahead without the company's representative because a bare sick note was no valid excuse.

The DPA required a hospital trust to comply with the Freedom of Information requests it previously failed to respond to in time and to devise and publish an action plan with measures to mitigate delays going further.

The DPA ordered a hospital trust to respond to the Freedom of Information requests it previously failed to reply to in time and to devise and publish an action plan with measures mitigating delays in the future.

The DPA ordered a travel blogger to comply with their ex-partner's request to erase their photos from the blog. However, the DPA dismissed the request for the erasure of the personal data of their children, considering it an issue to be resolved within a broader dispute on parental authority.

The DPA found a 360-degree employee feedback process unlawful because it lacked the works council agreement required under the Austrian Labour Constitution Act. The employer could not rely on contract or legitimate interests to circumvent this requirement.
The DPA reprimanded a market research consultancy firm for conducting robocall surveys that were deemed to be for direct marketing purposes without obtaining prior consent.

The Italian DPA investigated Enel Energia after a complaint from a customer who, despite being on the Public Opposition Register and refusing marketing consent, received many unwanted promotional calls following an electricity contract. Further reports showed that calls made for 'managerial' purposes turned into sales pitches without consent. The Garante found breaches of the principles of lawfulness and accountability, lack of valid legal basis and consent, and inadequate selection and control of telemarketing partners. It ordered corrective measures on processors and re-contact procedures and imposed a fine of EUR 563,052, plus publication of the decision.

A former employee complained that his ex-employer, the insurance mutual ITAS Mutua, had not properly answered his access request for the contents of his individual work mailbox after his employment ended. The Garante investigated and also found problems with the retention of email and internet browsing data for long periods, inadequate information to employees, and workplace-monitoring rules. It found violations of the GDPR principles, transparency, access and employment-data provisions, and of Article 114 of the Italian Code. It ordered full access for the complainant, ordered the company to bring its policies into line within 90 days, and imposed a fine of EUR 50,000.

During the evening TGLa7 news of 19 June 2025, a report on the 'Paragon' spyware case showed stock footage in which phone numbers, names of individuals, labels such as 'lover of' and details of calls and messages were legible. These data had nothing to do with the case. The Garante found the broadcast breached lawfulness and minimisation (Art. 5(1)(a) and (c) GDPR) and the journalistic essentiality principle. It declared the processing unlawful, banned further dissemination of the data, and fined La7 EUR 40,000, also ordering publication of the decision on its website.

A guardian of a care-home resident, using INPS's pre-filled ISEE service, saw the names of other residents of the same institution. INPS notified a data breach affecting 47,464 people living in registered communal residences, whose tax code, name and birth date were shown to 2,919 users. The Garante found two separate conducts unlawful. For the pre-loading of cohabitants' data into the pre-filled form it imposed a fine of EUR 40,000. For allowing minors to access the online DSU submission service it issued only a warning. No corrective measures were ordered since INPS had already fixed the problems.
